tags.name: Releases
tags.description:
A release is a snapshot of a project's configuration: one revision of
each resource, plus who made it, when, and from which commit. It points
at those revisions and never copies their content, which stays with
each resource's own endpoints.

Create a release from the files in your `.zitadel/` directory, or from
revision ids you already have. Creating a release doesn't deploy it,
and you can deploy the same release to any number of origins.

Every release carries a digest of its content, so you can check
whether the files you have are already released.

A release's content never changes. If it must never be served again,
revoke it. A release can't be revoked while any origin still serves
it.

rollback is another deployment: it re-deploys an earlier one with the
variable values it froze, and the deployments in between stay in the
history.

the first capability step. Creates a new session implicitly unless
`session_id` is provided, together with that session's `session_token`

The browser `Origin` header selects which deployment serves this attempt:
the gate admits the origin against the project's origin patterns and live
previews, the newest deployment to that exact origin is the target, and
that deployment's release supplies flow definitions, user schemas and
branding. The resolved deployment is sealed into the `_zflow` cookie so
later steps keep the same configuration. An origin that matches no pattern

parameter for all subsequent `/flow/{id}/submit` calls.

The response also sets an encrypted `HttpOnly` cookie (`_zflow`) containing

The server is stateless between requests — all flow state lives in this

post.description:
Submits user input for the current step. The server validates,
processes (e.g., verifies a credential), advances the state machine
through any invisible steps, and returns the next visible step.

The response sets an updated encrypted `HttpOnly` cookie (`_zflow`)
with the new flow state. The server is stateless — all orchestration
state is carried in this cookie between requests.

**Important:** The `id` in the response may differ from the `id` used in
the request. This happens when a flow pivots (pushes a new flow onto the
stack) or when a stacked flow completes (auto-pops to the parent flow).
Always use the `id` from the latest response for the next request.

## Flow completion

When `step.type` is `complete`, the flow is terminal. The `step.behavior`
field tells the frontend what to do:

| `behavior`   | Action                                                     |
|------------- |------------------------------------------------------------|
| `redirect`   | Navigate to `redirect_uri` (OIDC/SAML auth request done). |
| `show`       | Render the step as a success screen (e.g., registration).  |

A `complete` step is only returned when the **entire flow stack** is done.
If a stacked flow (e.g., recovery pivoted from login) finishes, the server
auto-pops to the parent flow and returns the parent's next step — the
frontend never sees a `complete` for intermediate flows.

## External sign-in

`{action: "sso", sso_provider_id, return_target}` on a step that offers
`sso_providers` returns the engine-emitted `sso-redirect` step, whose
`redirect_url` the frontend navigates to.

- The flow state does not change, but `_zflow` is re-sealed like on
  every response, so its ten-minute window restarts at this submission;
  the external sign-in and the return must complete within it.
- A second `Set-Cookie` line carries the browser-binding cookie the
  callback checks: `HttpOnly`, `Path=/`, `SameSite=Lax`.
- On every host except http loopback it is `__Host-_zsso` with `Secure`.
- When the request host is http loopback (local development, where
  Safari rejects `Secure`), it is `_zsso` with no `Secure`; the
  `__Host-` prefix is dropped because it requires `Secure`.

A connection whose `client_id` is a `${{ NAME }}` reference has it filled
from the project's variables. A provider the engine cannot start a
sign-in with, including a reference with no variable behind it,
re-renders the step with `error.sso_unavailable`.

Reuses the deployment sealed into `_zflow` at `createFlow`; it does not
re-resolve from `Origin`. If that release was revoked since the attempt
started, the response is `409` with `rel.revoked`.

- Audience-bound (requires matching project key for exchange)

Lists the people who can administer the project, and how each of them
gets that access. A person appears once, with one entry in `sources` per
way they hold it:

- `owning_team`: an active member of the team that owns the project
  (ADR 054 §2). Removing a grant does not remove this access; it ends
  only when the person leaves the team or the project changes owner.
- `grant`: an unexpired `admin` grant on the project, either to the
  person (`grant_id` only) or to a team they are an active member of
  (`grant_id` and `team`). Revoking that grant removes this source.

The list follows the authorization check: team membership is read from
the same membership projection the check expands, so a person who left a
team, or whose team or user was deactivated, is not listed through it.
Grants that expired or carry a lower role are left out. A person whose
only access is a `viewer` or `editor` grant is not an admin and is not
listed. Like the check, the list does not look at a person's user status
beyond that, so a direct grant to a suspended person is listed.

A person whose access comes only through teams the caller is not a
member of is left out, and a team the caller is not in is named by
`team_id` only. The grant to such a team still shows in the project's
grants.

session cookie (`sessionCookie`) that can read the project.

active, so provisioning will not clear it. What will depends on

untyped, so the values to expect are enumerated here:

    team or the user. A user deactivation cascades to that user's

    be active: what unblocks the claim is restoring the user's access,

Creates an anonymous session shell with no user and no factors (`state: building`).

This is optional — an `auth_attempt` will create a session implicitly if none is provided.
Use this explicitly when you want to:
- Pre-allocate a `session_id` before the user is known, so device/telemetry signals
  can be correlated with the eventual authenticated session from the start.
- Track anonymous state (bot detection, device fingerprint) that survives until authentication.

Creating a session is an app-plane operation on the project credential
(`session.write`). The returned `session_token` is a session credential for the
end-user client, not a management scope: it is delivered as the
`__Host-zitadel_session` cookie (`zitadel_session` over plain http to a
loopback host) and authorises the self-service operations
`GET /sessions/me` and `DELETE /sessions/me` (`sessionCookie` scheme). The
by-id operations `GET /sessions/{session_id}` and `DELETE /sessions/{session_id}`
are operator endpoints and require `session.read` / `session.delete` instead.

The `session_token` is superseded when a handoff exchange completes — clients must
replace it at that point.

Anonymous sessions expire aggressively (10-minute TTL). The TTL resets to the configured
full session TTL when the first authentication factor is written via a completing `auth_attempt`.

post.summary: Exchange handoff token for a session
post.description:
Consumes a one-time `handoff_token` minted by `POST /auth_attempts/{id}/handoff`
and returns the resulting session and a `session_token`.

The server resolves the originating `auth_attempt` from the token and then:

| Originating auth_attempt | Outcome |
|---|---|
| No `session_id` | A new authenticated session is **created**. |
| `session_id` points to an anonymous shell | Existing session is **upgraded** — user and factors written in, TTL reset to full session TTL. |
| `session_id` points to an active session (step-up) | Existing session is **upgraded** — new factors merged, `assurance_levels[]` expanded. |

The response shape is identical in all three cases.

The `session_token` supersedes any previously issued `session_token` for the same session.
Clients must replace their stored token at this point.

Requires a project service key (OAuth2 client credentials).

The project comes from the project secret. A query `project_id` that
disagrees answers `403` with `proj.mismatch`. The exchange resolves a
deployment the same way as other runtime operations; with no browser
`Origin` and nothing deployed to the resolved target the response is
`409` with `rel.not_deployed`. A revoked release answers `409` with
`rel.revoked`.

parameters.description:
Optional retry key for safe retries of the handoff exchange (Category B idempotency).
Retries carrying the same key within the exchange window return the cached session
payload without consuming the one-time handoff token again.

400.description:
Invalid request. A handoff token that is unknown, already exchanged, or
expired is refused with `sess.invalid_handoff_token`; the response does
not say which, and in each case the caller starts a new sign-in.

The `project_id` does not match the project the credential belongs to
(`proj.mismatch`).

exchange) is required, with the session's token from `GET /sessions/me/csrf`

and the cookie itself is cleared in the response.

another project is left alone, and so is its cookie.

read this response. It stays the same for the life of the session, so a

post.summary: Create or revise an identity provider connection
post.description:
Creates or revises a connection document. If the slug does not already
exist, a new connection is created. If a connection with that slug already
exists, a revision is created.

A revision gets a new `revision_id` and does not modify the connection
`id`, so identity links that reference the connection keep resolving while
releases and auth attempts stay pinned to the revision they captured.

Identity fields are fixed for the life of the connection and a revision
that changes one is rejected: `protocol`, `subject_claim`, and `issuer`,
the field that names the authority. Their values decide which provider
account a stored subject belongs to, so changing one would silently
repoint existing identities at a different provider.

`subject_claim` is optional, and `sub` is used as the default value. If a
revision updates `subject_claim` to a different value than the one set
during creation, the request is rejected.

OIDC is the only protocol.

The document is validated against the `idp-connection.json` schema before
anything is stored. The rules the engine applies when it starts a sign-in
then run on the document, so a connection that could never start one is
refused here instead with `idp.endpoints_partial`: the OIDC block sets an
endpoint without the others. It either sets no endpoint, and discovery
fills them, or sets `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, `jwks_uri`,
and `userinfo_endpoint`. `userinfo_endpoint` may be left out when
`id_token_mapping` is on, but setting it alone still counts as setting an
endpoint. The details list the missing endpoints.

A refused document stores nothing, and on a revise the current revision
stays unchanged.

revision, ordered by `created_at` (first publish) and then `id`. Filter
by `operation` to read the policy of one operation; a project that never
published one gets an empty list.

The lookup is scoped to the project in `project_id`.

passwordPolicy.summary: A project with a password policy

post.description:
Publishes the project's policy for an operation as a new immutable
revision, creating the policy on its first publish. The newest revision
applies to the next time the operation runs; nothing already stored is
re-evaluated, so a stricter password policy applies the next time a
password is set.

The request is typed by `operation`: an unknown operation or setting, or
a value of the wrong type or outside its bounds, answers `req.invalid`
like any malformed request. The operation's template then checks the
config again, together with the rules that relate settings to each other
(a `min_length` above `max_length`), and answers `pol.invalid`. Its
`details.details.violations` lists everything that failed, settings
first, then rules: `{"setting": "min_length"}` for one setting, or
`{"config_rule": "min_length_not_above_max_length", "settings":
["min_length", "max_length"]}` for a rule across settings, with the
settings it reads. A setting left out is off, and `{}` switches every
rule off; there are no defaults.

published.summary: The second publish of a password policy

post.description:
Evaluates a policy config against one request, without side effects, and
answers the decision the operation would reach. Nothing is read from or
written to the project: the config is the one in the body, checked
exactly as a publish checks it, so an invalid config answers `pol.invalid`
with the same violations.

`input` is what the operation's request carries, in the operation's own
terms (a password, not its length): the server derives what the policy
checks with the code the live operation runs, guards included. `facts`
states what the operation would look up at runtime, such as whether the
candidate matches one of the user's kept passwords.

The decision and the names of the failed rules hold wherever the
operation runs. `code` and `violations` are what an API call answers; a
login flow shows the same rules as field errors on the password field
(`error.x-auth-methods#password_<rule>` in `step.error`).

Which policy a project or release applies is not decided here: read it
and pass its config.

The caller needs read access to the project in `project_id`.

post.description:
Assembles a release from existing revisions, given as
`(kind, revision_id)` pairs. To build one from files on disk, use
`POST /releases/build`.

Each revision must exist in the project and is recorded under the handle
it declares. The release must be complete and consistent:

- Every handle its revisions name must be in the release: a flow's
  `user_schema`, and the IDP connections named by a flow step's
  `sso_providers` or a schema's `x-auth-methods.sso.providers`. A missing
  one answers `rel.unresolved_reference`, naming the resource and the
  handle, e.g. `flow_definition default-login: user_schema human-user not found`.
- Every flow is validated as on save, against the user schema revision
  in the release. A flow that fails answers `rel.invalid`, with the
  reason in `details`.

Idempotent on the set of revisions: the same revisions with a different
`message` answer `200` with the existing release. A new release answers
`201`. Creating a release does not deploy it.

person types the digest a transcript printed. The project holds at most
one release per digest, so the filtered list has one entry or none, and
an unknown digest is an empty list rather than an error. Paths take the
`rel_` id only; the matched entry's `id` is what to use there.

post.description:
Builds a release from the resources of `.zitadel/` as authored on disk,
grouped by kind, in one transaction: a failure anywhere leaves no
revision and no release. The caller records nothing.

If the project already holds a release with the same content, the same
`content_hash`, the request answers `200` with that release and
allocates nothing, however long ago it was built. Otherwise every resource is compared against the
project's newest revision of the same handle: unchanged content reuses
that revision, changed content allocates a new one, and the request
answers `201` with the new release. A policy whose config matches only an
older revision allocates a new one too, so a request that resolves no
release, which reads the newest revision, applies it as well. Metadata is excluded from the
comparison, so the same content under a different `message` is the same
release.

A structurally malformed request is refused while decoding with
`req.invalid`, naming the offending fields. A well-formed bundle is then
checked resource by resource, as each kind's create endpoint checks it,
and every failure is reported at once: the request answers `400` with
`rel.invalid`, and `details.resources` lists each resource that failed.
A handle that resolves neither in the bundle nor in the project answers
`rel.unresolved_reference`, naming the pointer and the handle.

Building writes revisions, so besides `release.write` it needs the write
scope of every kind the bundle carries a resource of: `schema.write`,
`flow_definition.write`, `branding.write`, `idp.write` and
`policy.write`, as the per-kind create endpoints do. A missing scope answers `403` with `rel.permission_denied`,
naming the kind. An empty kind needs no scope.

Building a release does not deploy it. A release is not tied to an
origin, and the same release can later be deployed to any number of
origins unchanged.

post.description:
Marks the release revoked, so that its content is never served again.
From then on the release cannot be deployed and is refused on every path
that would serve it, including to a build that pins its digest, with
`rel.revoked`.

A release that any origin still serves cannot be revoked. An origin
serves the release of the newest deployment to it, so the call answers
`409` with `rel.in_use`, naming each such origin and that deployment.
Deploy another release there or roll back first, then revoke. Revoking
therefore never takes an origin down. Deployments that named the release
earlier stay in the history.

Idempotent: revoking a release that is already revoked answers `200`
with the release unchanged, `revoked_at` still naming the first
revocation. There is no un-revoke; build a new release instead.

Takes no body. The lookup is scoped to the project in `project_id`, so a
release id of another project answers not found exactly as an unknown id
does.

Bind a user or team to `project.viewer`, `project.editor`, or
`project.admin` on the project identified by the `project-id` header.
Name the principal with `user` (`user_id` or `identifier`) or `team`
(`team_id` or `name`). IDs are `asgn_<opaque>`. Owning-team
(`project.team`) grants are not created here — claim owns that path. An
unrevoked grant with the same principal and relation occupies the unique
key even after `expires_at`; DELETE it before re-creating.
Create does not accept `expand`. The `user_id` and team locators
return 201, whose `user` / `team` carry only `user_id` / `team_id`,

already exists. Creating by `user.identifier` answers 202 with no
body on every outcome. Granting the session caller's own user is
`grant.invalid` on either user locator. Read the grant back for
identifier and display.

Accepts either a project secret (`oauth2`) or a user-bound Console
session cookie (`sessionCookie`). Session callers are authorized as
the human against the target project (home may differ). Cookie-authenticated
requests follow the scheme's CSRF rules (`sessionCookie`).

get.description:
Returns the project's variables, keyed by name, each with its value per
kind. With `kind`, only that kind's values are returned.

Secret values are not returned. A secret appears as `{"secret": true}`,
which says a value is held without disclosing it.

patch.description:
Enters, replaces and removes the project's variables for the requested
kind. Names not in the body are untouched. Existing deployments keep the
values they froze.

Without `kind`, a plain value is written for both kinds. A secret is
written for `primary` only and removes the name's `preview` value, so a
preview never keeps a plaintext copy; set a preview secret with
`kind=preview`. `null` removes the name from both.

A bare scalar enters a non-secret value. `{"value": …, "secret": true}`
stores the value encrypted under the project's active `secret` key, after
which it can be referenced but not read back. `null` removes the name
(RFC 7386), which is how several variables are removed in one request;
removing a name the project does not hold is a no-op rather than an error.

The body is applied whole or not at all, so a rejected request leaves the
project's variables exactly as they were. Writing the same name twice
replaces the value rather than duplicating it, which makes a retry safe.

post.description:
Makes a release live on its targets by recording a deployment,
atomically: on success every target serves the release and the record
exists; on failure nothing changes and no record is written.

Name the release by exactly one of `release_id` or `content_hash`; it
must already exist in the project. `targets` is `primary` or preview
URLs. The deployment freezes the project's variable values for its kind,
with no fallback between primary and preview values.

A deployment to `primary` changes nothing when the project's newest
primary deployment has the same release and frozen values and covers
exactly the current primary origins: the call answers `200` with that
deployment. Any other request writes a new deployment and answers `201`;
for preview URLs that record renews their previews.

Failures:
- `400 dep.invalid`: both or neither of `release_id` and `content_hash`;
  a primary origin named exactly; `primary` mixed with preview URLs;
  `primary` on a project with no primary origin; `ttl` with `primary`;
  `ttl` above 365 days (`P365D`).
- `400 dep.variables_missing`: a referenced variable has no value for
  the kind; `details` names the kind and every missing variable.
- `403 proj.origin_not_allowed`: a preview URL matches no preview
  pattern, or is a loopback URL.
- `404 rel.not_found`: the release id or digest names no release here.
- `409 dep.conflict`: `expected_deployment_id` is not the deployment
  this write replaces; `details.deployment` is that deployment.
- `409 rel.revoked`: the release is revoked.

sessionCookie.name: __Host-zitadel_session
sessionCookie.description:
The session cookie issued at session creation or superseding handoff exchange.

A browser holds it as `__Host-zitadel_session`, with `Secure`. Over plain
http to a loopback host (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`) the server sets it
as `zitadel_session` instead, without `Secure` or the prefix, so that Safari
keeps it, and accepts that name there too; `__Host-zitadel_session` takes
precedence. A program sends `__Host-zitadel_session` over any transport.

A missing or invalid cookie yields `401` with code `auth.unauthorized` and the message
`Missing or invalid session token.`

Cross-site request forgery (ADR 053 §5): a state-changing request that this
cookie authenticates must come from the same origin — a cross-site browser
request is refused with `403` and code `auth.csrf_invalid`. Every such
request must also send the session's token from `GET /sessions/me/csrf` in the
`X-Zitadel-CSRF` header, or it answers the same `403`. The only exceptions are
the `POST …/query` reads, which need no token. Safe methods (`GET`) are not checked. A request a project secret
authenticates is not affected.

active: The team is available for use.
deactivated: The team is no longer active but is retained for historical and audit purposes.

name.description: The name of the team.

updated_at.description: The time when the team was last updated.

lifecycle_owner_team_id.description:
The team that owns this user's identity lifecycle, or `null` when the
user is self-owned. This is a single team and a different concept from
the user's team memberships: it decides who may deprovision the user, not
which teams the user collaborates in. Memberships are their own paginated
resource — `GET /users/{user_id}/teams`.

lifecycle_owner_team.description:
The team named by `lifecycle_owner_team_id`, present only when the
request asked for it with `expand: ["lifecycle_owner_team"]` (ADR 059).
Absent means it was not requested; `null` means the user is self-owned
and there is no owner to resolve.

Requesting it does not guarantee it is present on every user. Today
`team.read` is checked once for the whole request, so it is; once that
check is per team, a page may contain a user whose owner the caller may
not read, and such a row answers with neither the team nor `null` —
`null` already means self-owned. What it answers with instead is decided
with the granular scopes (#420); do not read the two cases above as the
complete set.

This is the same representation `GET /teams/{team_id}` serves. It is a
single team, not a collection, so it carries no cap and no truncation
flag.

membership's participation state. The team's `name` travels with the entry, so
a page renders without a follow-up `POST /teams/query` per row.

Roster membership is not lifecycle ownership. A user can belong to many teams
while still owning their own lifecycle — that single owning team is reported
as `metadata.lifecycle_owner_team_id` on the user itself.

id.description: The unique identifier of the team.

name.description: The name of the team.

membership_status.description:

removed from are not returned.

created_at.description: The time when the user joined this team.

updated_at.description: The time when this membership was last changed.

user.title: User
user.description:
A user represents an individual identity in the system. It can be used to
represent a human user, but also a service account or any other type of
identity.

`attributes` is the document that satisfies the user schema named by
`schema`: its property names and types are defined entirely by that schema,
and it is what the schema validates. The rest of the object — `id`,
`schema`, `metadata` — is the server-owned envelope. Keeping the two apart
means a schema may name a property `id` or `metadata` without colliding with
the envelope, and closed-world keywords (`additionalProperties: false`,
`propertyNames`, `unevaluatedProperties`) behave as their author expects.

schema.description:
The schema that defines the content of `attributes`. These schemas can be
created using the `/schemas` endpoint. A default schema is provided.
This schema can be retrieved using the same endpoint.

identifier.description:
The current value of the user schema's designated identifier
(`x-identifier`), resolved live at read time. Absent when the schema
designates no identifier or the user carries no value for it.

identifier_property.description:
The schema property `identifier` came from, so clients can reach the
property's schema for semantics (a mailto link, a field label)
instead of guessing from the value. Present exactly when
`identifier` is.

display.description:
The `x-display` rendering — the designated properties' values joined
in list order, resolved live at read time. Purely presentational.
Absent when the schema designates no display properties or the user
carries no values for them. Clients render `display`, falling back
to `identifier`, then `id`.

teams.description:
The user's team memberships, present only when the request asked for them with
`expand: ["teams"]` (ADR 059). Absent means it was not requested; `[]`
means the user has none.

Deliberately outside `metadata`: memberships are a related collection, not
part of the server-owned envelope, and it is a different concept from
`metadata.lifecycle_owner_team_id` (ADR 024).

teams_truncated.description:
True when the user is on more teams than the embedded list carries. The
embedded list is capped and cannot be paged; read them all at
`GET /users/{user_id}/teams`. Present only alongside `teams`.

user-expand.description:
A related object to embed on each returned user (ADR 059).

- `teams`: the user's team memberships, as `teams` on each user. The property
  is omitted entirely when not requested and `[]` when the user has none, so
  "did not ask" is distinguishable from "there are none". Embedded lists are
  capped and are not paginated: past the cap the user carries
  `teams_truncated: true` and the whole list is read at
  `GET /users/{user_id}/teams`.

  Membership is team participation, not lifecycle ownership — the
  owning team stays at `metadata.lifecycle_owner_team_id` (ADR 024).

  Requires `team_membership.read` in addition to `user.read`.

- `lifecycle_owner_team`: the team that owns the user's identity lifecycle,
  as `metadata.lifecycle_owner_team`. It resolves the id already carried at
  `metadata.lifecycle_owner_team_id`, and serves the same representation as
  `GET /teams/{team_id}`. The property is omitted when not requested and
  `null` when the user is self-owned. One team, so no cap and no truncation
  flag.

  Requires `team.read` in addition to `user.read`.

The two are independent: asking for one says nothing about the other, and
neither implies the other's permission.

The scope requirements apply to project secrets. A Console session carries
no scopes; it may use both expansions when it may read the whole project
(the `viewer` role or above). A session whose grant covers only part of the
project still lists users, but an expansion is refused with
`403 user.permission_denied`.

user-sort-field.description:
Field to sort users by. Only stored columns are sortable: the keyset cursor
holds the last row's sort values, so a value computed per request would skip
or duplicate rows between pages.

Sorting by `lifecycle_owner_team_id` groups self-owned users together, since
the column is null for them.

user-filter-field.description:
Field to filter users by:
- `created_at`: RFC3339 timestamp
- `id`: user id
- `schema`: the schema the user's attributes satisfy, matched against the
  value the user carries as `schema`. Each revision of a schema has its own
  URL, so `equals` selects the users on one revision and `not_equals` the
  users on any other.
- `schema_object_type`: the `object_type` of the user's schema, which every
  revision of that schema shares. It may be repeated, like any field: give
  `not_equals` once per object type to exclude several. A schema without an
  object type reads as `""`, so `not_equals` matches its users and `equals`
  `""` selects them. Combine `equals` here with `schema` `not_equals` the
  newest revision to find the users still on an older one.
- `status`: one of `active`, `suspended`, `deactivated`, `pending_purge`
- `team_id`: restricts the result to users holding an **active** membership
  in that team. A user who has been invited but has not accepted does not
  match. `equals` is the only operation, and the field may be given once —
  this names one team, not a set.
- `lifecycle_owner_team_id`: the team that owns the user's identity
  lifecycle. The column is nullable for self-owned users, and a null filter
  value is rejected, so self-owned users cannot be selected by this field.

**The two team fields answer different questions.** `team_id` is membership:
which team the user collaborates in, readable per user at
`GET /users/{user_id}/teams`. `lifecycle_owner_team_id` is ownership: which
team may deprovision the user. A user can belong to many teams while owning
their own lifecycle, so the two disagree often and neither implies the other
(ADR 024).

`team_id` and `schema_object_type` are filterable but not sortable: neither
is a column on the user, so both are absent from the sort-field enum.

Filtering on `team_id` requires `team_membership.read` in addition to
`user.read`: it reads the same memberships that `expand: ["teams"]` embeds.
A Console session, which carries no scopes, may filter on it when it may read
the whole project (the `viewer` role or above); with a grant covering only
part of the project the filter is refused with `403 user.permission_denied`.

filter-value.description:
Filter-value specifies which values can be filtered by a query endpoint. This
is a union of types. When a value is specified which is not assignable to the
field which is being filtered, a 400 error will be returned.

filter-operation.description:
Filter operation defines the operations which can be used when filtering on a
query endpoint.

On text fields, `contains` is a case-insensitive substring match. `equals`
compares the whole value and is case-sensitive unless the field documents
otherwise.

patch-user-request.title: PatchUserRequest
patch-user-request.description:
A partial update, merged into the user's current state. At least one of
`schema` and `attributes` must be present; an empty patch is rejected with
`user.invalid`.

`attributes` is merged key by key into the stored attributes: an omitted
key stays untouched, an object merges recursively, `null` deletes the
attribute, and any other value replaces the stored one. The merged result
is validated as a whole against the user's schema, so a patch that deletes
or invalidates a required property is rejected with `req.invalid`.

`schema` moves the user to another registered schema — the ADR 009 §4
upgrade mechanism. The target must be a revision of the user's current
schema (the same `objectType`), newer or older; a schema of another
`objectType` is rejected with `user.invalid`. A schema stored without an
`objectType` is a revision of nothing, so a user cannot move to or from
one. The request must be
self-contained: merged attributes are validated against the new schema
before commit, and every uniqueness claim is recomputed under the new
schema's annotations. Values removed by an earlier move are not restored
by moving back.

The schema the user follows after this patch. Omit it to keep the

and be a revision of the user's current schema.

keys are untouched.

patch-my-user-request.title: PatchMyUserRequest
patch-my-user-request.description:
A partial update of the caller's own attributes, merged into the current
state: an omitted key stays untouched, an object merges recursively,
`null` deletes the attribute, and any other value replaces the stored one.
The merged result is validated as a whole against the user's schema.

Unlike `PATCH /users/{user_id}`, the schema pointer cannot be moved here:
schema upgrades are a management operation.

attributes.description:
The changed attributes only. `null` deletes an attribute; omitted
keys are untouched.

project-origin.title: ProjectOrigin
project-origin.description:
One of a project's origins: a pattern and what it is for. A `primary`
pattern is an exact origin (scheme and host, no `*`) that admits requests
from the URLs it matches. A `preview` pattern only bounds which URLs a
preview deploy may register; it may include at most one `*` inside a single
host label (`*` matches one or more characters, none of them a dot). A
literal beats a wildcard. Unknown hosts are accepted as written. An empty
list means every origin is admitted until the first pattern is added.
Loopback origins are admitted without a pattern.

password-hash-policy.description:
The method a project's passwords are hashed with. A project that has not set
one hashes with the server default, which is argon2id unless the deployment
configured otherwise.

This governs hashing only. Passwords already stored keep verifying under the
method they were written with. A policy change rewrites no stored password by
itself: a password moves to the new method on its owner's next successful
sign-in, or when its owner sets a new one.

algorithm.description:
The hashing algorithm. Only algorithms that can hash appear here; the
legacy encodings the server can still verify for imported users
(md5, phpass, drupal7) are not among them.

params.description:
The algorithm's cost parameters. Exactly the parameters the chosen
algorithm takes must be given: `time`, `memory` and `threads` for argon2i
and argon2id; `cost` for bcrypt and scrypt; `rounds` and `hash` for
pbkdf2 and sha2. A parameter another algorithm takes is rejected rather
than ignored, and a missing one is not filled in from a default, because
cost is the whole of a hashing method's strength.

The properties below are the union across algorithms, so which of them
apply, and for `hash` which of its values, depends on `algorithm`. They
are not modelled per algorithm here because the code generator renders a
conditional schema as an untyped object, which would cost every client
the types for the whole policy.

Values outside the limits the deployment configured are rejected, as is
an algorithm the deployment cannot verify: hashing with a method that
cannot be read back would lock out every user whose password was written
that way.

cost.description: bcrypt cost, or scrypt's log2 of the CPU/memory cost.

hash.description:
The underlying hash. pbkdf2 takes any of the values listed here; sha2
takes only `sha256` and `sha512`, because it is the crypt(3) scheme,
which has no other form. Any other combination is rejected with
`proj.password_hash_invalid`.

user-property.description:
The meta-schema one property of a customer's user schema is validated
against. The generated `user-property.json` adds
`allOf: [{$ref: draft-2020-12}]`, which cannot live here because code
generators choke on it.

Native JSON Schema keywords such as `type`, `format`, `title` and `writeOnly`
are accepted without being listed below. `writeOnly: true` is reserved for a
value that may be written but is never returned by the read API; nothing
enforces it today, so responses still include write-only properties.

x-unique.description: The level of uniqueness for this property, if applicable

x-claim.description: The claim name for this property, if applicable

Whether this property's value may appear in audit event payloads. Audit
payloads are deny-by-default: a property without this annotation

user-schema.description:

The generated `user-schema.json` adds `allOf: [{$ref: draft-2020-12}]`,
which cannot live here because code generators choke on it.

$schema.description: The JSON Schema version used for this schema.

objectType.description:
The type of user this schema describes. This is a customer chosen name.
Every revision of a schema shares its `objectType`, and flow
definitions name the schema they operate on by it.

metaSchema.description: The user Schema version used for this schema.

Path of the leaf property whose value identifies a user (nested leaves
are addressed by their dot-joined attribute path). The property must

discoverable credentials identify the user through the assertion
itself, so passkey-only and API-managed schemas may designate nothing;
flows using identifier-first passkey are validated at the flow level
instead.

Ordered leaf property paths whose values, joined with a space, render
the user's display name.

schema-document.description: The customer-authored JSON Schema document, served verbatim.

created_at.description: The time when the schema was created.

`GET /schemas` is asked for it with `expand=in_use`; omitted otherwise.

schema.title: Schema
schema.description:
A schema resource: the server-owned envelope around a customer-authored
JSON Schema document.

`schema` is the customer-authored document, served verbatim: its keys and
contents are defined entirely by its author. The rest of the object — `id`,
`metadata` — is the server-owned envelope. Keeping the two apart means the
document may declare any property (including `id` or `metadata`) without
colliding with the envelope, and the resource `id` stays distinguishable
from the document's own `$id`.

id.description:
The resource id: the server-minted `sch_*` identifier, or the
customer-supplied `$id` URI when the document declared one at creation.

challenge-nonce.description:
Origin-bound, single-use nonce obtained from `POST /bootstrap/challenge`.
Binds the request to the browser that initiated the flow, preventing
cross-origin replay.

session-proof-token.description:
The `session_token` of the session the request runs against, as
`POST /sessions` or `POST /sessions/exchange` returned it. It proves the
caller holds that session. Required with `session_id`, and must belong to the
same session and project; with `session_token` alone, the request runs
against the token's session. A missing, foreign, expired or revoked token is
refused with the same invalid-request error, whether or not the session
exists.

Name of a specific flow definition to use.
When omitted, the engine selects the best-matching definition

Set to true to simulate the flow without actually creating any
